profile.summary: IgLM is a generative language model for antibody sequences. Given an antibody heavy or light chain variable sequence with one span replaced by a mask, together with tags for the chain type and the species of origin, it generates replacement spans of variable length using the sequence on both sides of the mask, and it can also generate a whole chain from a short prompt or score an existing sequence. Its purpose is to build synthetic antibody libraries, for example diverse CDR loop libraries, from sequences that look like natural antibodies.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract and Methods: Infilling formulation; README: Command line usage

summary_quotes.text: We present Immunoglobulin Language Model (IgLM), a deep generative language model for creating synthetic antibody libraries.
IgLM formulates antibody design based on text-infilling in natural language, allowing it to re-design variable-length spans
We trained IgLM on 558M antibody heavy- and light-chain variable sequences, conditioning on each sequence’s chain type and species-of-origin.
IgLM supports sequence infilling, sequence generation (with prompting), and sequence evaluation from the command line.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: IgLM is a transformer decoder based on a modified GPT-2. A span of the antibody sequence is replaced by a single mask token, the remaining sequence is concatenated with a separator and then the span itself, and two conditioning tags for chain type and species are prepended, so an ordinary left-to-right language model learns to produce the missing span with the sequence on both sides available as context. In training the masked spans were ten to twenty residues long, chosen at random, so that spans of any position and length can be re-designed at inference. The released configuration is a 4-layer model with embedding size 512, 8 attention heads and a vocabulary of 33 tokens.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Two sizes were trained: IgLM and IgLM-S, which the paper describes as 13M and 1.4M trainable parameters; its hyperparameter table gives total parameters of 12,889,600 and 1,439,616. Both checkpoints are bundled in the Python package, which selects them by name, and IgLM is the default. A result should name the checkpoint, the package version (setup.cfg declares 0.1.0) or the commit, and the sampling settings, because generation is stochastic and the paper varies temperature and nucleus probability.

sections.title: What the authors report
sections.body: The paper reports that infilled CDR loop libraries had better in silico developability profiles than the parent antibodies and that sequences infilled by IgLM were typically more human-like than their parents by OASis identity. The authors also note, citing other work, that antibody-specific language models have been found to underperform universal protein models on antibody fitness prediction tasks. These are the authors' claims, not measurements by Rewire.

gaps: The sources do not state the inference hardware or memory needed. The paper gives only the training cost, about three days on four NVIDIA A100 GPUs, and the package picks a CUDA device when one is available.
No licence for the generated sequences is discussed, and the JHU agreement governs the software rather than model outputs.
The README command line examples point at a fasta file under data/antibodies/, which is not in the repository tree read here, so the Python package calls were used for the run guide instead.
The paper does not give a date for the Observed Antibody Space snapshot used, so the training cutoff is unknown.

run_guide.summary: Install the iglm package and re-design a CDR H3 span of an antibody, then score a sequence.
prerequisites: Acceptance of the JHU Academic Software License Agreement, which allows non-commercial use by non-profit academic or research institutions only.
Python with PyTorch 1.11 or above, Transformers 4.6.1 or above, tokenizers, biopython, numpy and tqdm, which setup.cfg declares as the dependencies.
A GPU is optional: the package selects a CUDA device when one is available and falls back to the CPU.
No data download is needed for inference: both checkpoints ship inside the package.

steps.title: Re-design a CDR H3 span
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
from iglm import IgLM

iglm = IgLM()

parent_sequence = "EVQLVESGGGLVQPGGSLRLSCAASGFNIKEYYMHWVRQAPGKGLEWVGLIDPEQGNTIYDPKFQDRATISADNSKNTAYLQMNSLRAEDTAVYYCARDTAAYFDYWGQGTLVTVS"
chain_token = "[HEAVY]"
species_token = "[HUMAN]"
infill_range = (98, 106)
num_seqs = 100

generated_seqs = iglm.infill(
    parent_sequence,
    chain_token,
    species_token,
    infill_range=infill_range,
    num_to_generate=num_seqs,
)
print(generated_seqs[:3])
PY
steps.explanation: The README's package example for infilling, wrapped in a shell heredoc. It loads the default IgLM checkpoint and generates 100 unique variants of the 1JPT heavy chain with a re-designed span from position 98 to 106. A final print of the first three sequences was added by Rewire so the step shows its result.

steps.title: Score a sequence
steps.shell:
python3 - <<'PY'
import math
from iglm import IgLM

iglm = IgLM()

sequence = "EVQLVESGGGLVQPGGSLRLSCAASGFNIKEYYMHWVRQAPGKGLEWVGLIDPEQGNTIYDPKFQDRATISADNSKNTAYLQMNSLRAEDTAVYYCARDTAAYFDYWGQGTLVTVS"
chain_token = "[HEAVY]"
species_token = "[HUMAN]"

log_likelihood = iglm.log_likelihood(
    sequence,
    chain_token,
    species_token,
)
perplexity = math.exp(-log_likelihood)
print(log_likelihood, perplexity)
PY
steps.explanation: The README's package example for sequence evaluation, wrapped in a shell heredoc, with a print of the two values added by Rewire. It returns the log likelihood of the sequence under the given chain and species conditioning and the corresponding perplexity.

The command line entry points iglm_infill, iglm_generate and iglm_evaluate exist as console scripts, but the README examples for them use a fasta file under data/antibodies/ that is not in the repository tree read here.
Generation is stochastic: the number of sequences, the temperature and the nucleus probability change the result, so a run should record them.

notes: The weights are not on Hugging Face: both checkpoints are committed inside the pip package, so the weights URL in the structured rows is the repository itself. The licence is the JHU Academic Software License Agreement, which has no SPDX identifier, so it is recorded as custom-noncommercial and the source entries carry no licence field; nothing fetched for this record may be redistributed, so every source has store_bytes false. The record's existing source is the TorchCraft benchmark paper (torchcraft-20261115-source-arxiv-v1), which is not an IgLM source and was not read here. The paper copy saved is the PubMed Central author manuscript of the Cell Systems article; no release date for the checkpoints is stated in the files read, so released is null.
